comment_text: How would you feel if I wrote a poem about what it's like to live in Alaska, even though I've never visited that place? How would you feel if I made a movie about what it's like to grow up as a black kid in New York, even though I'm white? It would be fucking offensive. It would be disgusting. Even if the art I produced was technically skillful, it would be a lie. Everyone who likes AI art doesn't seem to understand this. Even if AI art appeared technically skillful (it currently doesn't) it would be fundamentally opposed to art. It would be an insincere mimic at best. It would only have value because it copied the value of something else, and it would be inferior to that thing it copied. Procedurally generated patterns can be beautiful, and if AI ever produces art that is better than an inferior placeholder, it would be something like that; something that explores the parts of existence that aren't necessarily tied to a human life.

Making the jaw a millimetre less sharp, the eyes elevated by a micrometer and even the thinkness of the strokes can change the emotion the subject conveys. comment_text: My solution to the controversy. 1) No, AI art will never take the job of artists fully. Rather,  artists will adapt to use AI in their own way. That said, there is a possibility of accidental plagiarism,  when the picture is obviously based on a specific work, but that can be easily resolved by just performing research before posting your image and redoing it.  3) We can make AI not the whole process, but only the parts of it that we choose. Like, if I'm making a webseries, I can make  a soundtrack, a story, the dialogues, the world building myself, and use AI for voiceover. Nice to look at but there’s nothing in those eyes. One has a very decisive emotion behind it that is easy to relate to.  Art is not about creating beautiful things. Art often does result in beautiful things though because of what it actually is. It’s a means of human connection. It’s a form of communication between ourselves to display visceral ideas that we ourselves can’t be put any other way.  If art simply was just a means of creating “good images”, then yeah, sure. AI has “solved” art. We don’t need it anymore.  AI may be able to recreate the “ghibli style” or make hyper realistic images or have incredible shading, but it can’t conceive and invent something like Picasso’s Guernica, or the emotional weight of something like a Rothko painting. AI couldn’t think of signing a toilet and calling it art.  Dare I say, AI couldn’t think of something like taping a banana to a wall with duct tape.  Why?  Because these statements are windows into the minds of their creator.  Humans depend on connection. We need each other. Left on our own, we can not survive. We’re social creatures, introverted as some of us are. Art is a means of true human connection.  An AI could maybe write a really catchy melody. Four AI bots, however, couldn’t hang around each other in Liverpool, dreaming up romantic songs about their young lives in the 60s and express their joy to the world in the way they did. An AI might be able to write some surreal imagery and put it to an acoustic guitar. But it can’t pull together the experience and the single creative vision behind something by Bob Dylan. Heck, AI could ABSOLUTELY randomize white noise for 2 hours. But it can’t do it with the intentionality and the natural, human ebbing and flowing of someone like Merzbow. It can take a bunch of old records and maybe sorta cobble it together into an audio piece about dementia. But it couldn’t have the human heartbreak and empathy to create something like those final few minutes of The Caretaker’s EATEOT (which I think I’ve only heard 2 seconds of… but oh man, those 2 seconds…).  AI could end a cartoon episode about a fear of the outdoors in a silly way. But it takes a uniquely strange and funny group of people to end it with a guy in a gorilla suit literally smacking a wooden chair wwe style into an animated starfish and squirrel SUPPOSEDLY “in a bag” and then immediately stop when the talking sponge asks what the heck it’s doing underwater with a reveal that a family was watching the episode on TV in utter bewilderment.  It’s why when you talking about reading someone’s books or poems, you often refer to them as reading T.S. Elliott. You’re reading Dickinson. You’re reading Kafka. You’re reading Tolkien. You’re reading THEM. That’s what you’re there to read. Not in a parasocial way (hopefully), but in a way that you emotionally engage with their thoughts. You’re not there for the book itself: the collection of words in and of themselves.  AI, in this instance, only knows how to write the book. The final thought is that the only constant in the world is change. Adaptation is the key to survival. One of the ways to better ride the rollercoaster of change is to perhaps look at our economic system and reconsider the inherent inequalities in it.
